title: The YM2608 OPNA registers
covers: the registers of the YM2608 (OPNA) as Yamaha's application manual describes them, and what MAME does for each

rows.text: Unlike the FM registers, the SSG registers can be read as well as written.
The SSG part pronounces three rectangular waves at once, each with a duty of 1:1.
A channel's tone frequency is ftone = phiM / (64*TP), with phiM the master clock and TP the 12-bit tone period setting.
Registers $00, $02 and $04 are the fine tune of channels A, B and C: the 8-bit part of the 12-bit tone period.
Registers $01, $03 and $05 are the coarse tune of channels A, B and C: the 4-bit part of the 12-bit tone period.
The tone period TP ranges from 1 to 4095, so ftone ranges from phiM / 262,080 to phiM / 64.
The SSG part also has a noise generator with a pseudo random waveform, and its frequency is set by the noise generator control.
The noise frequency is fnoise = phiM / (64*NP), with NP the 5-bit noise period setting.
Register $06 is the noise period: the 5-bit setting NP.
Register $07 holds the bits that switch the tone and the noise of each channel on or off and set the I/O mode of the two general-purpose I/O ports.
The bit table of $07 reads IN/OUT for ports B and A, then !NOISE for channels C, B, A and !TONE for channels C, B, A.
D7 and D6 control the I/O direction of the two I/O ports; the capture's wording suggests 0 is input and 1 is output.
D5 to D3 set the noise output of channels C, B and A (in the capture's table order); a 0 outputs it.
D2 to D0 set the tone generator output of channels C, B and A (in the capture's table order); a 0 outputs it.
Registers $08 to $0A control the output level of channels A, B and C.
The output level is either fixed, at a constant volume, or follows an envelope that changes it over time.
D4 selects the mode: 0 gives the fixed output level set by D3-D0, 1 makes the level follow the envelope generator.
D3-D0 set the output level, the maximum with all 1; when D4 is 1 these bits are don't care.
Table 3-1 weights the level bits 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1 for DAC data L5 to L1, maximum level 31; the capture is garbled.
The 5-bit logarithmic DAC gives 16 steps in fixed mode, from the upper 4 data bits, and 31 steps in envelope mode (0 and 1 equal).
With a channel in envelope level mode, the output level follows the envelope shape in time; the cycle and the repetition are set in the following registers.
Register $0B is the fine tune of the envelope period EP.
The repetition frequency of the envelope generator is fEG = phiM / (1024*EP), with EP the cycle set in $0C and $0B.
The cycle tEG is 1/fEG.
The bit table of $0C and $0B is headed Coarse Tune over Fine Tune.
Register $0C is the coarse tune of the envelope period EP.
Register $0D sets the envelope waveform: its four bits D3-D0, named C, ATT, ALT and HLD in the capture, select one of eight envelopes.
Each envelope waveform equals the SSG-EG waveform of the FM sound source part (page 31 of the manual).
A write to $0D also sets m_envelope_state to 0.
The SSG part has two general-purpose I/O ports, usable as an extension port between the CPU and an external system.
Registers $0E and $0F store the I/O data of ports A and B; with a port used as an output, the CPU writes the data.
With a port used as an input, the data of the external system is set for the CPU to read.
The capture's bit table labels the ports $0D and $0E, which disagrees with its own heading, $0E and $0F.
Before reading or writing $0E and $0F, set the I/O mode in D7 and D6 of $07.
A port in output mode keeps outputting the data written until new data replaces it, except after initial clear or a change to input mode.
While OPNA is in initial clear (!IC) the I/O ports are in input mode.
Do not apply an input voltage to the I/O terminal while the port is in output mode.
MAME hands each byte written in output mode to ymfm_external_write, but its write cases have none for 0x07, so switching a port to input calls no handler.
The rhythm part plays six basic drum tones made with ADPCM voice synthesis, all six at once, each with its own level setting.
The rhythm registers are $10 to $1D, and their data can be accessed when bus control signal A1 is 0.
A write to $10 switches rhythm tones on and off by event: D5-D0 name the tones and D7 (DM) says key on or dump.
D7 (DM) at 1 dumps the named tones, forcing them silent; at 0 the named tones key on.
D5-D0 name the tones, one bit each: RIM, TOM, HH, TOP, SD and BD from D5 down to D0 in the capture's table.
A keyed-on tone decays naturally by the envelope of that rhythm tone.
A key-on or a dump of a tone that is still decaying takes effect at the timing of the new event.
Register $11 is the integrated volume of the rhythm part.
The total level is controlled in 64 steps from -47.25 dB to 0 dB, with a resolution of 0.75 dB.
D5-D0 are the 6-bit rhythm total level RTL.
With D5-D0 all 0 the level is -47.5 dB, while the sentence above gives the range as -47.25 to 0 dB (the capture reads '-47.25-OdB').
With D5-D0 all 1 the level is 0 dB.
The attenuation table gives 24, 12, 6, 3, 1.5 and 0.75 dB for D5 to D0; its layout is garbled in the capture.
With RTL 0, (RTL ^ 0x3F) is 63, so vol is at least 63 and MAME's channel output returns before adding any sample to the outputs.
Register $12 is a register for the test of OPNA.
A write to register $12 is for the test of OPNA.
The initial value of the test register $12 is all 0.
Registers $18 to $1D set the output channel and the level of each rhythm tone: 32 steps from -23.25 dB to 0 dB, resolution 0.75 dB.
Registers $18 to $1D each hold L and R (D7, D6) and the instrument level IL (D4-D0) of one rhythm tone.
The attenuation table gives 12, 6, 3, 1.5 and 0.75 dB for D4 to D0.
D7 at 1 outputs the tone to the left channel.
D6 at 1 outputs the tone to the right channel.
With D4-D0 all 0 the level is -23.25 dB.
With D4-D0 all 1 the level is 0 dB.
$18 is BD (bass drum), $19 SD (snare drum), $1A TOP (top cymbals), $1B HH (high hat), $1C TOM (tam-tam) and $1D RYM (rim shot).
MAME turns a sum of 31 steps into gain mul/2^shift of 8/256 against 15/32 at 0 steps, about -23.5 dB.
MAME's ADPCM-A register reset sets the registers written at 0x18 to 0x1D to 0xDF: both outputs on and the instrument level at its maximum.
Register $21 is the register for the test of OPNA.
The test register is not used in a user application.
LFO is a built-in low frequency oscillator that modulates the operators to give the sound a periodic change; OPNA's is a sine wave.
The sine-wave LFO was enabled in hardware by the function added to the OPN (YM2203).
Register $22 sets the oscillation frequency of the LFO and its on or off.
D3 at 1 turns the LFO on.
D2-D0 set the LFO speed, its oscillation frequency.
The timer part holds two kinds of presettable timers and flags that start, stop and control them.
When the time set in a timer passes, its timer flag (D1, D0 of status 0 and 1) is set to 1 and an IRQ is generated for the CPU.
Timer A is a counter with a resolution of 9 us at phiM = 8 MHz, made from 10 bits held in $24 and $25.
Register $24 holds P9 to P2, the eight high bits of the 10-bit timer A value.
The timer A interval is tA = 72 * (1024 - NA) / phiM, with NA from 0 to 1023 and phiM the master clock.
With phiM = 8 MHz, tA is at most 9216 us and at least 9 us.
Register $25 holds P1 and P0, the two low bits of the 10-bit timer A value.
Bits D7 to D2 of $25 are marked / in the capture's table.
Timer B is a counter with a resolution of 144 us at phiM = 8 MHz, made from the 8 bits of $26.
Register $26 holds P7 to P0, the 8-bit timer B value.
The timer B interval is tB = 1152 * (256 - NB) / phiM, with NB from 0 to 255 and phiM the master clock.
Timers A and B are controlled by the timer controller $27.
Register $27 is the timer controller; its bit table is headed MODE, RESET, ENABLE and LOAD, with B and A for the timers.
D1 and D0 start and stop the timers (B and A in the capture's table order): 1 starts a timer and 0 stops it.
D3 and D2 control the timer flags of status 0 and 1.
At 1 a timer overflow sets the timer flag.
The timer flag also generates the interrupt signal (LOW) on the !IRQ terminal.
At 0 a timer overflow leaves the timer flag unchanged.
D5 and D4 at 1 reset the timer flags of status 0 and 1.
The D5 and D4 bits are cleared to 0 at the same time.
D7 and D6 set the mode of channel 3: normal, CSM or effect sound; the capture garbles the codes of the last rows.
In normal mode channel 3 pronounces like the other channels.
In CSM mode the F-Number is set for each of the four slots, and key on and off are done with timer A.
In effect sound mode a separate F-Number can be set for each slot, as in CSM.
MAME's mode write hands the written byte to the register store as it is.
MAME computes the IRQ as set when the status flag survives the AND with m_irq_mask and the inverted register status mask, so a masked timer flag raises no IRQ.
Register $28 does the key assign of each channel: a channel number and the on or off of each of its four slots.
D4 to D7 are the on or off of slots 1 to 4.
D2-D0 name the channel: 000 channel 1, 001 channel 2, 010 channel 3, 100 channel 4, 101 channel 5, 110 channel 6.
When D7 (SCH) of $29 is 0, channels 4 to 6 cannot be assigned.
The key assign of each channel is done by specifying the channel and switching its slots on or off.
MAME's key-on decode adds 3 to the channel number when D2 is set on an OPNA; the decode names no SCH test.
Register $29 holds SCH in D7 and the IRQ enables in D4 to D0.
D7 (SCH) sets the number of sounding channels: 0 gives 3 channels (CH1-CH3, OPN mode), 1 gives 6 at once (OPNA mode).
The value of SCH is 0 after initial clear.
To pronounce six channels at once, set SCH to 1 first.
IRQ ENABLE: when a bit of D4-D0 is 1, the IRQ terminal goes low with the generation of the corresponding status flag.
The default of D4-D0 is 1.
MAME's branch for 0x29 sets no channel count from D7 (SCH): the byte goes to m_irq_enable and only its low five bits reach the IRQ mask.
MAME also clears the bits set in m_flag_control from the IRQ mask, and that starts at 0x1c, so at reset only D1 and D0 of 0x29 can raise the IRQ.
The prescaler sets the dividing value n of the internal operation clock of the FM and SSG parts: phiINT = phiM / n.
The capture says only these registers ($2D to $2F) write the address data and the prescaler is set.
Address $2D selects FM 1/6 and SSG 1/4 of the master clock, for a master clock up to 8 MHz (in the capture's table order).
After initial clear the prescaler is FM 1/6 and SSG 1/4.
The prescaler works on the FM and SSG parts only.
Use the default prescaler when accessing all the OPNA sound sources; the rhythm and ADPCM sampling rates are given for phiM = 8 MHz.
MAME sets the FM prescale to 6 for $2D; for the SSG it configures the output resampler, 4 to 3 for prescale 6 at medium fidelity.
MAME takes the default prescale 6 from the FM engine's constructor; ym2608::reset does not set the prescale again.
Addresses $2D and $2E together select FM 1/3 and SSG 1/2 of the master clock (in the capture's table order).
For $2D and $2E together the maximum master clock is 4 MHz.
MAME sets the FM prescale to 3 when $2E is written at prescale 6; for the SSG it configures the output resampler, 2 to 3 at medium fidelity.
Address $2F selects FM 1/2 and SSG 1/1 of the master clock (in the capture's table order).
For $2F the maximum master clock is 2.67 MHz.
MAME sets the FM prescale to 2 for $2F; for the SSG it configures the output resampler, 1 to 3 for prescale 2 at medium fidelity.
Registers $30 to $B6 hold the tone parameters of each operator (slot) and of each channel; Table 2-2 gives the register address of each parameter.
A channel is specified by bank changing with the bus control signal A1.
Table 2-2 lists the register addresses of the slot parameters (DT/MULTI, TL, KS/AR, AM/DR, SR, SL/RR, SSG-EG) per channel and slot, in the columns S1 S3 S2 S4.
Registers $30 to $3E hold the Detune and Multiple parameters.
Multiple sets the magnification applied to the frequency information made from F-Number/Block.
Multiple values 0 to F give the magnifications 1/2, 1, 2, 3 up to 15 (Table 2-5).
Detune gives a slight shift of cycle to the frequency information made from F-Number, by a value that follows the Key Code obtained from F-Number.
Detune values 0 to 7 give FD 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, -1, -2, -3; D6 is a sign bit (Table 2-6).
The detune frequency shift in Hz is tabulated for each block, note and FD.
The output control circuit sets a whole level for the envelope made from the EG parameters; the resolution over the 96 dB range is 0.75 dB.
The output level is expressed as an amount of attenuation, with the operator's maximum output taken as 0 dB.
Registers $40 to $4E hold the Total Level (TL).
Total Level 00 is 0 dB (utmost level) and 7F is 96 dB of attenuation (minimum level).
The attenuation weights of the Total Level bits D6 to D0 are 48, 24, 12, 6, 3, 1.5 and 0.75 dB (Table 2-9).
The envelope generator (EG) is where volume and tone change over time from the start of the sound to its end; EG parameters are set per operator.
The envelope is shown by the attack, decay, sustain and release rates and the sustain level (Figure 2-4).
The envelope shape is exponential when attacking and a straight line at the other rates.
AR (Attack Rate) sets the speed to the utmost level after key-on, in 32 steps; larger AR makes the sound rise faster (the capture's last clause is garbled).
Registers $50 to $5E hold KS and the Attack Rate.
The same envelope rate at every pitch can sound unnatural, so the key scaling function changes the envelope rate according to the interval.
KS (Key-Scale) is set in registers $50 to $5E in four steps.
At KS 0 the key scale does not function.
The differences grow most at KS 3.
Table 2-8 lists the key-scaling value of the rate by KS, block and note; the capture's table layout is garbled.
The key scale changes the envelope rate according to the pronunciation interval: the rate shortens for higher pitches, which gives the tone a natural feeling.
Each rate is Rate = 2R + Rks (0 when R = 0), with R = 2 * RR + 1 for the release rate; Rate is capped at 63.
MAME adds the key code shifted right by KS xor 3 to each nonzero rate, capped at 63, so at KS 0 up to 3 is still added.
DR (Decay Rate) sets the speed of the fall from the utmost level to the sustain level, in 32 steps; a larger DR attenuates faster (remark on 0 garbled).
Registers $60 to $6E hold AM and the Decay Rate.
AMON in registers $60 to $6E switches the amplitude modulation of each slot on at 1.
SR (Sustain Rate) sets the speed of attenuation from the sustain level, in 32 steps; a larger SR attenuates faster, and at 0 the sustain level continues.
Registers $70 to $7E hold the Sustain Rate.
SL (Sustain Level) is the attenuation level where decay changes to the sustain rate, in 16 steps; larger SL gives more attenuation, and 0 gives none.
Registers $80 to $8E hold the Sustain Level and the Release Rate.
The attenuation weights of the Sustain Level bits D7 to D4 are 24, 12, 6 and 3 dB, and all four bits at 1 give 93 dB (Table 2-7).
RR (Release Rate) is the speed of attenuation after key off, in 16 steps; a larger RR attenuates faster.
The envelope generator can be controlled with the envelope shapes of the SSG part, which gives changes the EG parameters alone cannot.
To use SSG-EG, set AR to 1F; DR, SR and SL then decide the envelope change while keyed on, and RR works as usual for the time after key-off.
Registers $90 to $9E hold the SSG-EG value in D3 to D0.
The SSG-EG table lists eight shapes, numbers 0 to 7, for D3 D2 D1 D0 from 1000 to 1111.
Table 2-2 lists F-Num1 at $A0, $A1 and $A2.
Registers $A0 to $A2 hold F-Num1 (D7 to D0).
The F-Number/Block data are to be set according to the following procedure.
The F-Number/Block data are set by writing Block/F-Num2 to $A4-$A6 first, then F-Num1 to $A0-$A2.
MAME stores nothing for a write to $A3, $A7, $AB or $AF: the handler returns false before any store.
The music scale is shown by the interval within an octave (F-Number) and the octave (Block), which makes eight octaves easy to make.
The F-Number for a note is calculated from the note frequency, the master clock and Block; the capture's formula and its A4 example are garbled in places.
Registers $A4 to $A6 hold Block and F-Num2: the F-Number is 11 bits, 8 low and 3 high, and Block is 3 bits.
This data is common to the channel, and the four operators are given the same information.
Table 2-2 lists Block/F-Num2 at $A4, $A5 and $A6.
Table 2-4 gives example F-Numbers for phiM = 8 MHz, octave 4 and A4 = 440 Hz, with the F-Number bits and the key code division.
The key code gives the key scaling of the envelope rate and the detune; it is set by a division of the octave based on the F-Number combined with Block.
N4 = F11; N3 = F11(F10+F9+F8) + !F11 F10 F9 F8; the 5-bit Key-Code is made from Block (B3, B2, B1), N4 and N3.
Table 2-2 lists *F-Num1 with A9, A8, AA and A2; the capture does not keep the row's columns.
The capture refers to a page for the mode setting of channel 3; the page number is not readable.
MAME stores nothing for a write to $AB: the handler returns false before any store.
Table 2-2 lists *Block/F-Num2 with AD, AC, AE and A6; the capture does not keep the row's columns.
$A8-$AA and $AC-$AE are the registers that set the frequency information when channel 3 is made the effect sound mode or the CSM voice synthesis mode.
Therefore they are not used in the usual pronunciation mode.
Table 2-2 lists FB/Algorithm at $B0, $B1 and $B2.
The way the operators are connected is the algorithm; eight can be selected, each slot works as modulator or carrier, and the fourth slot is always a carrier.
Choosing the algorithm best suited to the target tone is the first step of making a sound; the slot parameters are set afterwards.
The first slot of each channel has self feedback, which feeds its own output back as modulation; the return rate has 8 steps, 0 to 7.
Registers $B0 to $B2 hold the feedback modulation level and the algorithm.
Table 2-3 gives the feedback modulation levels 0 to 7 as OFF, pi/16, pi/8, pi/4, pi/2, pi, 2 pi and 4 pi.
Figure 2-3 names the eight algorithms 0 to 7, from the four serial connection mode to the four parallel sine synthesis mode.
Table 2-2 lists L/R, AMS/PMS at $B4, $B5 and $B6.
PMS sets the depth of the phase modulation by the LFO for each channel, which gives a periodic change of pitch to the frequency set with F-Number/Block.
AMS sets the depth of the amplitude modulation by the LFO for each channel, a periodic change of the operator's output level.
Registers $B4 to $B6 hold L, R, AMS and PMS.
PMS 0 to 7 gives a modulation level of 0, 3.4, 6.7, 10, 14, 20, 40 and 80 cent.
AMS 0 to 3 gives a modulation level of 0, 1.4, 5.9 and 11.8 dB (the last value has a page number glued on in the capture).
L and R are the switches for the left and right output of the FM sound source part.
L and R, bits D7 and D6 of $B4-$B6, are on at 1 and output the channel to that side.
MAME's reset sets $B4, $B5 and $B6 of both register banks to 0xC0, which switches both outputs on.
The bus control columns read 0 0 1 0 1 for the data below.
In that read, addresses 00-0F read the data of the SSG registers.
In that read, address FF reads the device identification code.
MAME returns the value 1 as the device identification code.
The ADPCM part is controlled by registers $00 to $10, which are accessed when bus control signal A1 is 1.
An external memory in the text means the RAM or ROM that OPNA manages.
Control register 1, $00, controls the start of ADPCM voice analysis/synthesis and the external memory access.
Register $00 holds START in D7, REC in D6, MEM DATA in D5, REPEAT in D4, SP OFF in D3 and RESET in D0.
D0 is a reset function at ADPCM voice synthesis: at 1 a running synthesis is stopped and returns to the initial state.
Make REPEAT (D4) 0 when resetting.
D3 makes the terminal SPOFF 1 at 1; it is used as a speaker-off control signal when ADPCM analysis and AD conversion are done.
D4 sets the repetition: at 1 the same address section of an external memory is accessed repeatedly and ADPCM voice synthesis is done.
D5 selects the memory accessed for ADPCM analysis/synthesis data; the capture's wording on the CPU-managed memory is garbled.
D6 is 1 when analysis data is written into an external memory, from ADPCM voice analysis or from the CPU.
D7 is the setting bit that starts ADPCM voice analysis/synthesis; with an external memory the operation starts when 1 stands in it.
All the conditions needed for analysis/synthesis must be set before it starts.
With CPU-managed memory the operation starts when the ADPCM-DATA register $08 is read or written.
RESET and REPEAT work only when an external memory is accessed.
The capture's note on making the START bit 0 and resetting the remainder of the data is garbled.
A $00 write with D0 set clears MAME's internal playing flag and sets ready, plus end of sample if it was playing; buffer and address are not reset there.
MAME writes external memory from a $08 write when D7 is clear and D5 and D6 are set (the agreeing half); with D6 set its clock returns early.
MAME starts synthesis at a $00 write when D0 is clear and D7 is set (the agreeing half); with D6 set its clock returns early.
MAME starts synthesis at a $00 write (D0 clear, D7 set) whatever D5 is; a $08 write with D7 set clears ready only when D5 and D6 are clear.
Control register 2, $01, specifies the external memory and the control and output of DA/AD conversion of ADPCM.
Register $01 holds L and R in D7 and D6, and SAMPLE, DA/AD, RAM (TYPE) and ROM in D3 to D0.
D0 selects the external memory, ROM at 1 and DRAM at 0, and D1 selects the DRAM access, 8 bit at 1 and 1 bit at 0.
D2 selects the conversion, DA at 1 (data written in the DAC DATA register $0E) or AD at 0, and D3 starts it when made 1.
D6 at 1 outputs to the L channel and D7 at 1 outputs to the R channel (the bit table above lists L before R).
DA conversion starts when SAMPLE (D3) and DA/AD (D2) are made 1 in control register 2; AD conversion starts when SAMPLE is made 1 with DA/AD 0 and SPOFF 1.
MAME uses D0 to choose the address shift: 5 when D0 is 1; with D0 clear, 5 when D1 is 1 and 2 otherwise.
MAME stores a $01 write and prints D2 as the DAC enable in the log message of a $00 write that starts playback.
MAME takes D7 as pan left and D6 as pan right, and adds the sample to output 0 for pan left and to output 1 for pan right.
Registers $02 (low) and $03 (high) hold the start address.
The address setting of start/stop is laid out as BANK, CAS ADDRESS and RAS ADDRESS fields.
The address figure shows the start address followed by 0 0 0 0 0 and the stop address by 1 1 1 1 1.
For DRAM the BANK is the chip selection of eight DRAM.
For DRAM of 256k x 1 bit the minimum addressing resolution is 32 bits (4 bytes).
At ROM and 8-bit DRAM access, the BANK data D7-D5 is set to the same value in the start and stop address.
At ROM and 8-bit DRAM access, data is accessed by byte and the minimum addressing resolution is 32 bytes.
The start address and the stop address of DRAM and ROM are set.
Registers $04 (low) and $05 (high) hold the stop address.
$06 and $07 specify the sampling frequency when AD (including ADPCM analysis) and DA are converted, in the range 2 kHz to 16 kHz.
Registers $06 and $07 hold PRESCALE(L) and PRESCALE(H), 11 bits in all: N10 to N0, with N10 to N8 in the high register.
fsample = phiM / 2NPRE with NPRE = 250 to 2047 at phiM = 8 MHz; for example NPRE = 500 gives 8 kHz.
MAME advances playback by the delta-N value of $09 and $0A, and prints the prescale in the log message of a $00 write that starts playback.
The ADPCM data register is at address $08.
Register $08 is the ADPCM DATA register, D7 to D0.
MAME returns the next byte from memory only when D7 and D6 of $00 are clear and D5 is set; every other read of $108 returns 0.
$08 is a buffer register for ADPCM data into which the CPU can write when it accesses an external memory; the capture's sentence is garbled.
ADPCM data is 4 bits, so a byte holds two data.
In a byte the high 4 bits are the nth data and the low 4 bits are the next data, n+1.
MAME's $08 write clears ready with D7 set and D5, D6 clear; writes memory with D7 clear and D5, D6 set; otherwise with D7 clear it acts as a read.
Registers $09 (L) and $0A (H), DELTA-N, set the sampling frequency at ADPCM voice synthesis.
The same setting also gives the coefficient for linear interpolation between samples, which the capture ties to 55.5kHz.
DELTA-N is 16 bits d15 to d0: $0A holds DELTA-N(H) and $09 holds DELTA-N(L).
DELTA-N = (fsample/55.5kHz) times a power of two the capture prints as 216, whose exponent is doubtful; DELTA-N=9447 at fsample=8kHz.
Register $10, FLAG control, controls each flag of status 1.
After the system is reset, D4, D3 and D2 are initialized to 1 and the other bits are 0.
The bit table of $10 reads IRQ RESET at D7 and MASK ZERO, BRDY, EOS, TIMERB, TIMERA at D4 to D0.
D0 at 1 masks the flag of timer A whatever timer A does; the flag is taken as 0.
D1 at 1 masks the flag of timer B in the same way as D0 does for timer A.
D2 at 1 masks the EOS flag.
With the EOS mask set, the EOS flag is not generated at the ends of ADPCM analysis or synthesis, external memory read or write, and AD conversion.
D3 at 1 masks the BRDY flag.
With the BRDY mask set, the data writing and reading demand flags of ADPCM analysis, synthesis and external memory access are not generated.
D4 at 1 masks the ZERO flag.
Writing 1 to D7 makes the mask bits D4 to D0 disregarded and makes all status flags 0 at the same time; rewriting the bit is prohibited.
The capture also puts 0 in parentheses: each flag of status 0 is controlled too.
MAME's read of status 0 (offset 0) returns the timer flags without using m_flag_control; the mask is applied in the read of status 1 (offset 2).
With D7 set MAME calls the engine's set_reset_status(0, 0xff) and the ADPCM-B channel's clear_status for the EOS and PLAYING flags, and does not store m_flag_control.
MAME reads register 0x30 plus the operator offset, which adds 0x100 for each group of 12 operators.
MAME stores the byte written to this range in the FM register array at that register number.
MAME takes a write to the upper address port as 0x100 ORed with the data, and its upper data port sends addresses above 0x110 to the FM engine.

searched.gave: ymfm_opn.h and ymopn.h cite no manual; the comments in ymfm_opn.h only list the register bit layout.
The YM2608 manual in the table mentions channels 4 to 6 in Table 1-1 and in the CH4 to CH6 columns of Table 2-2, which first-bank entries own.
The bitsavers Yamaha components folder lists YM2149, YM2151 and YM2203 sheets and no YM2608 manual.
archive.org ym-2608-j-1 is the document table's archive copy of the Japanese manual; the capture used is the English translation.
No datasheet index was consulted: the manual already in the table is the maker's document for the chip.

MAME stores the byte written to this range in the FM register array at that register number.
MAME takes a write to the upper address port as 0x100 ORed with the data, and its upper data port sends addresses above 0x110 to the FM engine.

archive.org ym-2608-j-1 is the document table's archive copy of the Japanese manual; the capture used is the English translation.
No datasheet index was consulted: the manual already in the table is the maker's document for the chip.

rows.text: MAME reads register 0x50 plus the operator offset, which adds 0x100 for each group of 12 operators.
MAME stores the byte written to this range in the FM register array at that register number.
MAME takes a write to the upper address port as 0x100 ORed with the data, and its upper data port sends addresses above 0x110 to the FM engine.

rows.text: Register $0B, level control, sets the output level of ADPCM voice synthesis from no sound (00) to maximum volume (FF) in 256 steps.
The level data is effective only to the ADPCM voice synthesis output.
$0B holds LEVEL CONTROL, a byte D7 to D0.
Registers $0C (L) and $0D (H) set the limit value of the memory.
When the memory is accessed and the address gets to the limit address, it returns to 0.
The capture says the limit is equal to the stop address or assumed to be a large value, and read/write of the memory must be set; its wording is garbled.
The limit address is 16 bits: $0D holds LIMIT ADDRESS(H) and $0C holds LIMIT ADDRESS(L).
Register $0E, DAC data, is the register that DA conversion takes its data from: the conversion is done by writing data in it.
The data format written to $0E is two's complement 8-bit PCM data.
Register $0E is DAC DATA, a byte D7 to D0.
$0F is a register only for reading: it stores the data converted when AD is converted, and the CPU collects the PCM data by reading it.
The data format of $0F is two's complement 8-bit PCM data.
The bit table of $0F reads D7 to D0 over PCM DATA.
A read of $0F returns 0 in MAME: the ADPCM-B read handler starts from 0 and fills it only for a read of $08 in one mode.
